title: Sixth Word The Two Mens Responses And Outcomes

questions.question: In the comparison, what did the king place in the care of each of the two men?
questions.answer: Each man was given an estate along with the equipment and resources needed to run it.

questions.question: What was the condition of the time in which these men were living?
questions.answer: It was a dangerous and unstable period marked by conflict and upheaval.

questions.question: Why did the king send a high-ranking representative to the two men?
questions.answer: He sent him to deliver a merciful message about how they could protect what had been entrusted to them and gain from it.

questions.question: What was the central offer made to the two men?
questions.answer: They were asked to hand over the entrusted property to the king.

questions.question: According to the message, what would the king do with the property if they gave it back to him?
questions.answer: He would preserve it for them, keep it from being wasted, and later return it in a better form.

questions.question: How did the king describe his treatment of the trust after it was handed over?
questions.answer: He said he would treat it as though it belonged to them and would pay them generously for it.

questions.question: What did the king promise concerning the tools and machines?
questions.answer: He promised they would be used in his service and that their return would be multiplied greatly.

questions.question: Why did the king say he should take responsibility for expenses and supplies?
questions.answer: He said the two men were too needy and unable to cover the costs of such major work on their own.

questions.question: Until what point would they keep the income and benefit from the arrangement?
questions.answer: They would keep it until the time when military service ended.

questions.question: What warning was given if they refused the offer?
questions.answer: They would be unable to hold on to what they had, would lose it without benefit, and would also miss the price being offered.

questions.question: What would happen to the valuable instruments if the offer was rejected?
questions.answer: They would lose their worth instead of being put to good use.

questions.question: Besides losing the property, what other burden would fall on the one who refused?
questions.answer: He would struggle to manage and protect the trust and would also face punishment for mishandling it.

questions.question: What higher status did the king promise to the one who accepted?
questions.answer: He would serve under the king with honor instead of remaining in a low and restricted position.

questions.question: How did the wiser of the two men respond to the king’s message?
questions.answer: He accepted it gladly and with gratitude.

questions.question: What personal qualities led the second man to refuse?
questions.answer: He was proud, self-centered, and morally careless.

questions.question: What false assumption shaped the second man’s decision?
questions.answer: He acted as if he would remain in his estate forever and ignored how unstable worldly life is.

questions.question: What happened to the first man after his acceptance?
questions.answer: He rose to a high rank, received the king’s favor, and lived in happiness.

questions.question: What happened to the second man after his refusal?
questions.answer: He lost both joy and possessions and ended up in punishment and misery.

questions.question: What contrast between the two men forms the main lesson of the passage?
questions.answer: Accepting the king’s offer brings honor, safety, and reward, while rejecting it brings loss, humiliation, and suffering.

questions.question: How many men are at the center of the comparison, and what was each one given?
questions.answer: There are two men, and each received an estate with the necessary tools and resources.

questions.question: What does the unstable wartime setting suggest about the security of worldly possessions within the story itself?
questions.answer: It suggests that what people hold can easily be ruined, changed, or taken away.

questions.question: What does the king’s mercy show in the way he dealt with the two men?
questions.answer: It shows that he wanted their good and offered them a way to avoid loss and gain much more.

questions.question: What action did the king ask from the two men regarding the property in their hands?
questions.answer: He asked them to transfer it back to him.

questions.question: What future benefit did the king promise after the time of conflict had passed?
questions.answer: He promised to return what they had entrusted in a better state than before.

questions.question: How did the king reassure them about ownership and compensation?
questions.answer: He said he would count the trust as theirs and pay them a great price for it.

questions.question: In what way would the use of the workshops and tools become more beneficial under the king’s arrangement?
questions.answer: Their use would bring a vastly multiplied return and profit.

questions.question: What human limitation did the king mention to explain why his support was necessary?
questions.answer: He pointed to their poverty and inability to meet the demands of the work by themselves.

questions.question: What practical help did the king promise in addition to payment?
questions.answer: He promised to cover expenses, provide equipment, and still let them receive the gains.

questions.question: What does the phrase about five kinds of gain contribute to the message of the decree?
questions.answer: It emphasizes that accepting the offer brings many layers of benefit, not just one.

questions.question: If someone rejected the king’s offer, what did the king say would happen to the property itself?
questions.answer: It would slip away and be lost without any lasting benefit.

questions.question: What two kinds of loss would come from refusing the high price?
questions.answer: The person would lose both the property and the generous compensation attached to it.

questions.question: How would refusal affect the value of the fine equipment?
questions.answer: Those precious items would become worthless.

questions.question: What moral failure is attached to refusing the king’s offer?
questions.answer: It would amount to betraying something entrusted to one’s care.

questions.question: What distinction did the king make between low service and honored service?
questions.answer: He contrasted an ordinary and constrained status with an elevated position under a great ruler.

questions.question: How did the first man’s response show wisdom?
questions.answer: He recognized the goodness of the offer and accepted it thankfully.

questions.question: How did the second man’s character distort his judgment?
questions.answer: His pride and attachment to pleasure made him reject what would have saved him.

questions.question: What worldly realities did the second man fail to take seriously?
questions.answer: He ignored the disasters and upheavals that make worldly holdings temporary.

questions.question: What final outcomes prove that the first decision was right and the second wrong?
questions.answer: The first man ended in honor and happiness, while the second ended in loss, blame, and suffering.

questions.question: What basic situation begins the comparison in this passage?
questions.answer: A king entrusts two men with estates and the means to manage them.

questions.question: Why is the environment of the story important to understanding the king’s message?
questions.answer: Because the unstable environment explains why the property is at risk and why a better plan is needed.

questions.question: Who delivered the king’s message to the two men?
questions.answer: A noble representative sent by the king.

questions.question: Was the king’s message mainly a threat, a business offer, or a rescue plan? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: It was mainly a rescue plan presented in the form of a beneficial offer.

questions.question: What did the king ask the two men to do with what had been entrusted to them?
questions.answer: He asked them to return it to him through a voluntary transfer.

questions.question: Why did the king say this transfer would be better for them than keeping the property themselves?
questions.answer: Because he could preserve it, improve it, and reward them, while they could not protect it on their own.

questions.question: How did the king increase the attractiveness of the offer regarding the tools and machinery?
questions.answer: He promised that using them under his authority would bring far greater returns.

questions.question: What does the king’s statement about their poverty imply about the men’s condition?
questions.answer: It implies that they were dependent and lacked the ability to sustain such responsibilities by themselves.

questions.question: What three forms of support did the king promise concerning the work?
questions.answer: He would provide the expenses, supply the needed equipment, and grant the profits.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about trying to hold worldly things without the king’s arrangement?
questions.answer: It suggests that such an attempt is doomed to fail because those things do not remain secure.

questions.question: What would happen to the precious materials if left outside the king’s plan?
questions.answer: They would lose their purpose and value.

questions.question: Why would the one who refused deserve punishment according to the message?
questions.answer: Because he would misuse and fail to safeguard what had only been entrusted to him.

questions.question: What new identity would the accepting man receive under the king?
questions.answer: He would become an honored officer serving under the ruler.

questions.question: Which of the two men showed humility, and how can you tell?
questions.answer: The first man did, because he accepted the offer with gratitude rather than acting possessive.

questions.question: Which inner traits are linked to the second man’s refusal?
questions.answer: Pride, selfishness, and moral looseness.

questions.question: How did the second man’s view of time contribute to his downfall?
questions.answer: He behaved as if his stay in the estate would never end, so he ignored the reality of change and loss.

questions.question: What happened socially to the first man after his choice?
questions.answer: Others looked at his condition with admiration and envy.

questions.question: What happened socially to the second man after his choice?
questions.answer: Others felt sorry for him, though they also saw that his downfall came from his own mistake.

questions.question: What cause-and-effect lesson does the ending teach?
questions.answer: Wise surrender to rightful authority leads to honor and joy, while arrogant refusal leads to ruin and punishment.

questions.question: At the start of the passage, what does each of the two subjects receive from the king?
questions.answer: Each receives an estate together with the equipment needed for use and management.

questions.question: What does the story say about the lasting nature of things in that age?
questions.answer: Nothing remained secure; things were likely to disappear or be altered.

questions.question: Why does the king’s action count as merciful rather than merely authoritative?
questions.answer: Because he intervenes to protect the men from loss and to increase their benefit.

questions.question: Through whom does the king communicate his will?
questions.answer: Through an honored lieutenant.

questions.question: What is the first major reason the king gives for asking them to hand the property over to him?
questions.answer: He says he can keep it safe from pointless destruction.

questions.question: What improvement does the king promise after the period of war ends?
questions.answer: He promises to give it back in a better condition than it had before.

questions.question: How does the king combine generosity with authority in his offer?
questions.answer: He asks for the property back but also offers payment, preservation, and multiplied returns.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the men’s ability to finance the large responsibilities attached to the estates?
questions.answer: It says they are too poor and incapable to meet those costs.

questions.question: What does the king offer to carry on their behalf?
questions.answer: He offers to take on the expenses and provide the necessary means.

questions.question: What does the king still allow them to receive even after taking over the management?
questions.answer: He allows them to receive the income and profit.

questions.question: What is one direct consequence of refusing the king’s offer concerning preservation?
questions.answer: The person would not be able to keep the property safe.

questions.question: What is one direct consequence of refusing the offer concerning value?
questions.answer: The valuable equipment would lose its worth.

questions.question: What is one direct consequence of refusing the offer concerning accountability?
questions.answer: The person would be punished for violating the trust.

questions.question: In terms of rank, what difference separates acceptance from refusal?
questions.answer: Acceptance raises a person into honored service, while refusal leaves him low and disgraced.

questions.question: What made the first man “more intelligent” in practical terms?
questions.answer: He saw the wisdom of exchanging temporary control for lasting gain and accepted the offer.

questions.question: How is the second man’s pride described in a way that shows its extremity?
questions.answer: His ego is portrayed as swollen with arrogance to an excessive and rebellious degree.

questions.question: What illusion led the second man to dismiss the king’s decree?
questions.answer: He acted as though his possession and pleasure would continue forever.

questions.question: What result did the first man enjoy after a short time?
questions.answer: He attained high standing, royal favor, and a happy life in the king’s palace.

questions.question: What result did the second man suffer after a short time?
questions.answer: He was reduced to a miserable state, lost what he had, and endured punishment.

questions.question: What shared responsibility did the two men begin with in the story?
questions.answer: Both were entrusted with property and the means to operate it.

questions.question: How does the story describe the larger setting in which this trust was given?
questions.answer: It describes a turbulent time in which things were uncertain and exposed to loss.

questions.question: What does the king’s decree invite the men to do?
questions.answer: It invites them to turn over the entrusted property to him willingly.

questions.question: What purpose did the king give for this invitation?
questions.answer: He wanted to preserve the property for them instead of letting it be wasted.

questions.question: What future restoration did the king promise?
questions.answer: He promised to return it later in a better form.

questions.question: How did the king sweeten the offer beyond mere preservation?
questions.answer: He added generous payment and greatly increased returns from the use of the equipment.

questions.question: What does the king’s mention of their neediness reveal about their dependence?
questions.answer: It reveals that they could not independently handle the burdens tied to the trust.

questions.question: According to the decree, who would handle the major costs if they accepted?
questions.answer: The king would take responsibility for them.

questions.question: What would the men continue to receive while the arrangement lasted?
questions.answer: They would continue receiving the gains and benefits.

questions.question: What is one reason the king gives for why refusal makes no sense?
questions.answer: Because the men do not have the power to hold on to the property anyway.

questions.question: If they kept the trust for themselves, what would happen to the offered payment?
questions.answer: They would lose the chance to receive it.

questions.question: What would happen to the carefully made tools and precious materials if not used under the king’s plan?
questions.answer: They would become useless and lose their value.

questions.question: Why would the rejecting man face both stress and punishment?
questions.answer: Because he would struggle with protecting the trust and would also answer for betraying it.

questions.question: How does becoming the king’s soldier change a man’s status in the story?
questions.answer: It raises him from a low and constrained position to an honored and freer one.

questions.question: What emotional tone marks the first man’s response?
questions.answer: Thankfulness and glad acceptance.

questions.question: What emotional tone marks the second man’s response?
questions.answer: Defiance and possessive pride.

questions.question: What mistaken worldview can be inferred from the second man’s words and behavior?
questions.answer: He thought his control and enjoyment of worldly things would last permanently.

questions.question: How did the first man’s decision affect his final standing?
questions.answer: It brought him honor, favor, and a joyful life close to the king.

questions.question: How did the second man’s decision affect his final standing?
questions.answer: It brought him loss, humiliation, and painful consequences that others saw as deserved.

questions.question: What did the king initially entrust to each of the two subjects?
questions.answer: He entrusted each one with an estate and the necessary resources connected to it.

questions.question: What feature of the age made the king’s offer especially urgent?
questions.answer: The age was unstable and full of conflict, so possessions were not secure.

questions.question: What does the sending of a noble lieutenant suggest about the king’s approach?
questions.answer: It suggests that the message was important, dignified, and meant for the men’s benefit.

questions.question: What was the king asking the two men to surrender?
questions.answer: He was asking them to surrender what they were holding in trust.

questions.question: What reason did the king give for taking the property back into his care?
questions.answer: He could safeguard it and prevent it from being lost uselessly.

questions.question: What did the king promise to do once the conflict ended?
questions.answer: He promised to return the property in an improved condition.

questions.question: How did the king frame the arrangement financially?
questions.answer: He promised a high payment and greatly multiplied returns from the use of the tools.

questions.question: What limitation in the men did the king point out?
questions.answer: They were poor and unable to bear the expenses of the work.

questions.question: What responsibilities would the king assume if they agreed?
questions.answer: He would provide the costs and the needed equipment.

questions.question: What benefits would still come to the men during this period?
questions.answer: They would receive the income and profit.

questions.question: What does the king say about the possibility of preserving the property without his arrangement?
questions.answer: He says that no one can truly keep hold of it in that unstable situation.

questions.question: What double loss comes from refusal according to the decree?
questions.answer: The person loses the property itself and also loses the generous compensation.

questions.question: What happens to the specialized tools and precious materials if left outside the king’s service?
questions.answer: They decline in value and fail to fulfill their purpose.

questions.question: Why is punishment mentioned along with the loss of property?
questions.answer: Because refusing the offer means mishandling something that was only entrusted, not truly owned.

questions.question: What honorable role is offered to the one who accepts the king’s terms?
questions.answer: He is offered a respected military role under the king.

questions.question: How does the first man demonstrate sound judgment?
questions.answer: He recognizes the wisdom of the offer and embraces it with gratitude.

questions.question: How does the second man demonstrate spiritual and moral blindness within the story?
questions.answer: He lets arrogance and attachment to enjoyment keep him from seeing the danger around him.

questions.question: What happened to the first man in the end, and what does it show?
questions.answer: He rose in rank and lived in favor, showing that trust and submission brought success.

questions.question: What happened to the second man in the end, and what does it show?
questions.answer: He fell into misery and punishment, showing that pride and refusal lead to ruin.
